opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that LEACE, which stands for LEAst-squares Concept Erasure, is designed to be as surgical as possible. The guarantee we prove is that after erasure, no linear classifier can predict the concept from the representation better than a constant predictor. And among all transformations that achieve that guarantee, LEACE changes the representation as little as possible, in a least-squares sense. So it's the minimal edit that removes the linearly available information about the concept.

What that means for performance is roughly this: if the model's downstream behavior doesn't really depend on that concept, you'd expect very little damage, because you've only removed a low-rank slice of the representation. For a binary concept it's essentially rank one, so you're removing one direction's worth of information out of thousands. And empirically that's mostly what we see. When we erase something like gender from BERT embeddings, or part-of-speech information at every layer of a language model, perplexity goes up, but in a way that tracks how much the model was actually relying on that concept.

That's part of what makes it useful as an interpretability tool, not just a fairness tool. If you erase part-of-speech information and the model's performance degrades significantly, that's evidence the model was using linearly encoded part-of-speech features to do its job. And since the edit is minimal, you can be more confident the damage comes from removing the concept, not from collateral damage to unrelated features, which is a real problem with cruder methods like iteratively projecting out classifier directions, as INLP does.

I should add a caveat. LEACE is a linear guarantee. A nonlinear probe might still recover the concept, and the network's later layers are nonlinear, so in principle the model could still access some of that information. So when performance barely changes, that doesn't prove the model never used the concept. It might be using it in a nonlinear way we haven't touched. But the linear case is a natural starting point, especially given the evidence that a lot of the features models use really are linearly represented.

r001.rationale: It says erasing part-of-speech information could significantly degrade performance as evidence the model used it, but does not report that this substantially happened in the experiment.

r002.rationale: It mentions erasing gender from BERT embeddings and says perplexity goes up, but does not say the effect was tentatively small.

r003.rationale: It explains that performance may change little because LEACE removes a low-rank slice—one direction for a binary concept—from a representation with thousands of dimensions.

fable-5.1.text:
So the first thing to say is that LEACE is a surgical intervention, and the surgery is deliberately minimal. The guarantee we prove is that after applying the transformation, no linear classifier can recover the concept from the representation better than chance. And we show it's the least-squares-optimal affine map that achieves that. So in a sense you're changing the representation as little as you possibly can while still wiping out the linearly available information.

Now, the interesting question is what that does downstream, and I think there are really two regimes to talk about.

The first is the kind of thing we did in the paper with part-of-speech information in a language model. We erase part-of-speech from every layer's residual stream, concept scrubbing we called it, and you look at how much the loss goes up. And the answer is: it goes up, noticeably, but the model is nowhere near destroyed. And that's informative in both directions. The fact that it goes up at all tells you the model is actually using linearly encoded part-of-speech information to make predictions, it's not just an epiphenomenon that a probe happens to pick up on. But the fact that it doesn't fall apart tells you the model is not relying solely on that linear subspace. There's redundancy, there's nonlinear encoding, there are other features that are correlated with the thing you erased that can partially compensate.

And I'd emphasize, this is a much more honest measure of concept usage than just training a probe. Probing tells you the information is there. Erasure tells you whether removing it matters. Those are different questions, and historically people conflated them.

The second regime is where you erase something the model is really leaning on, and then you can see quite dramatic effects. The way I think about that is, you're essentially projecting out a direction, or a small set of directions, and if the next layer's computation is heavily dependent on reading from that direction, you've cut a wire. And the model doesn't have a graceful fallback.

There's a subtlety here though that I think is worth flagging. Because LEACE is defined with respect to a specific concept labelling, what you're actually erasing is "the linear information about these labels," and that includes anything that happens to be correlated with the labels in your dataset. So if your concept is confounded with something else the model needs, you'll damage performance for reasons that have nothing to do with the concept you care about. We tried to be careful about that, but it's a general limitation of any erasure method, not just ours.

And then the last point, which is maybe the most important caveat: linear erasure doesn't mean the concept is gone. It means it's not linearly recoverable. A later layer with a nonlinearity can in principle reconstruct it from features that were individually uninformative. So when we see a performance hit from concept scrubbing, I read that as a lower bound on how much the model depends on the concept, not the full story. If you want the full story you need something stronger, and that's part of why we've been moving toward things like the quadratic version, where you also match second moments and make the concept harder for a quadratic classifier to recover. But even that is a bound, not a proof that the information is absent.

So the short answer is: the damage is real but usually modest, that modesty is itself evidence about how distributed the model's representations are, and you should always interpret the effect as "what happens when you remove the linearly accessible part," not "what happens when the model forgets the concept."

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between making a concept linearly inaccessible and removing everything the model knows about that concept. LEACE gives you the former: it applies a transformation to the representations so that a linear predictor can no longer recover the concept, while changing those representations as little as possible.

What that does to performance depends on how the model was using the information. If performance drops, that’s evidence that the information removed by the intervention mattered for the task. But it doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve isolated a clean, self-contained concept, because the information can be shared with other useful features.

And if performance doesn’t drop, you shouldn’t conclude that the model never used the concept. There could be redundant information, or information that’s still accessible nonlinearly. So I’d interpret it as a fairly precise intervention on linear information in a particular representation, rather than literally deleting an idea from the model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between removing information and removing the model’s ability to use that information in a particular way. LEACE removes linearly accessible information about a concept from a representation, while changing the representation as little as possible. It doesn’t guarantee that the concept is gone in every possible sense—a nonlinear predictor might still recover it.

So if performance drops after erasure, that’s evidence that the information you removed was useful for the task. But it’s not automatically evidence that the model was using that concept in exactly the way you had in mind. The concept could be correlated with other useful information that the intervention also affects.

And if performance doesn’t drop, that doesn’t necessarily mean the concept was irrelevant. The model might have redundant ways of solving the task, or later layers might reconstruct the information. I’d treat LEACE as a fairly controlled intervention that helps you investigate those questions, rather than a definitive test of whether a model understands or uses a concept.
